explanations.explanation: It signals the end of a structured text fragment—a sentence‐ or list item–ending period—that acts as a boundary marker, letting the model switch contexts for what follows.

The feature appears to signal that the current token is a high‐activation subword prefix—a fragment that strongly cues a specific completion (often in proper names or compound terms) so that the model is primed to append the expected suffix (e.g. “ver” to complete “Denver”) rather than switching to an unrelated token.

It’s a signal for subword‐ or morpheme‐completion—that is, the model is “flagging” a token fragment (like a stem or affix) that needs to be properly stitched to its following piece to form the intended complete word.

It appears that this feature is marking tokens that are “incomplete” parts of a compound or contraction—i.e. a signal that the current word is meant to attach to a following clitic or morpheme (such as the “’t” in “don’t” or the rest of a split word like “paltry”). In short, the feature encodes a morpho‐syntactic marker for fused, joint tokens rather than standalone words.

It appears to be a circuitry that “notices” a sentence‐ or list‐ending period—marking a formal boundary so that the model then expects the start of a new sentence or a specialized enumerative token (often a numeral or capitalized word). In short, the feature is a sentence boundary (or punctuation‐boundary) indicator whose presence steers next‐token predictions toward context‐appropriate “restart” tokens, while its removal causes a fallback (“e”).

It appears that this feature “fires” on the beginning fragments of stylized, evaluative, often branded or proper‐name tokens (like “Ama…” in “Amazing” or “Den…” in “Denis/Denver”), which in context tend to initiate a promotional or headline‐style description. Its activation shifts the model’s continuation away from a causal “cause” and toward more descriptive, list‐ or punctuation‐driven completions.

It’s detecting a sentence‐or segment–ending punctuation marker—a signal that a thought or named entity has just closed, which then guides the model’s next-token generation (for example, triggering a change in capitalization or punctuation).

It appears that this feature is detecting and representing an alternative‐or disjunctive construction—a signal that the context is setting up a choice, contrast, or list of options (as in “and/or” or other alternative‐enumeration structures), which then biases the model to continue in a way that preserves that disjunctive meaning.

It’s a feature that “lights up” on formulaic, structured boilerplate text – the kinds of metadata or legal/document‐header snippets (with dates, copyright/legal phrasing, numerical specifications, etc.) that signal a formal or fixed-format text segment.

It appears that this feature is sensitive to strong end‐of‐segment punctuation—a marker that a sentence or title segment has just closed—which then shifts the predicted continuation. In short, it encodes the boundary (or “terminal punctuation”) signal that prompts the model to change its style and next‐token distribution.
